result.title: Improving semantic equivalence in research-level math formalization
result.comment: Accepted at the 6th Math-AI workshop at NeurIPS'26
result.summary: Formalizing mathematics in Lean is never a word-for-word translation of a paper: a Lean formalization changes definitions, strengthens hypotheses, splits arguments, and adds lemmas the paper never mentions. It stands to reason that a model that is good at autoformalization must be a good predictor of how a natural language source must differ from its faithful Lean formalization. With that in mind, we collect 4{,}076 audited examples of such changes from 832 Lean projects that formalize research-level mathematics, and use them to ask a practical question: how well can a model \emph{write} Lean inside a real research-level project that may contain tens of thousands of lines of code, and does training on discrepancies between natural language sources and their faithful Lean formalizations help? Our training set consists of 3{,}431 tasks from 141 repositories, and the test set consists of 645 tasks from the remaining 27 repositories. Training on in-project Lean nearly doubles complete proofs ($11\% \to 20\%$) and raises the share of statements in gold agreement with the project's own formalization by nearly a third ($30\%$ to $39\%$). The gain comes from the pairs themselves: an adapter trained only to predict how the Lean will differ, or a model told the difference in advance, barely helps. Training on where formalizations depart from their sources is thus an effective way of improving semantic equivalence in research-level formalization.

AI.brief_summary: 论文从 832 个 Lean 项目收集 4,076 条自然语言原文与忠实形式化之间差异的审计样本，用其中 3,431 个任务训练模型在真实研究级项目中写 Lean，并在留出仓库上测试，完整证明率由 11% 升至 20%。
AI.relevance_reason: 其「预测原文与形式化如何偏离」的辅助监督思路可能对应 latent 推理中的状态转换监督，而该辅助 adapter 几乎无效的负结果可供核查辅助目标在训练中的实际贡献。
